title: What Is Money?
description: Functions of money, commodity vs fiat, M0–M3, why money is whatever we say it is

concepts.title: The Functions of Money
concepts.contentHtml:
Money is defined by what it does, not what it's made of. Three classical functions:

Medium of exchange: something everyone accepts in trade. Without money, you'd need a 'double coincidence of wants' for every transaction — barter at scale is hopeless.

Unit of account: a common ruler for prices. Without money, comparing 1 chicken to 3 books to half an hour of legal advice is exhausting.

Store of value: a way to save purchasing power for later. Money lets you separate earning from spending across time.

Anything that fulfills these three roles is money. Historical examples include gold, silver, salt, cattle, shells, and cigarettes (in prisons and POW camps). Most of these eventually fail — at scale, modern fiat currency outperforms.

concepts.title: Commodity Money
concepts.contentHtml:
Commodity money has intrinsic value — gold has industrial and ornamental uses; cattle can be eaten or worked.

The advantage: limited supply makes it hard for governments to inflate. The Romans, the Spanish, and many other empires that debased coin currencies eventually paid through inflation.

The disadvantage: supply isn't tied to economic needs. A booming economy may run short of money even when it needs more transactions; a gold-standard recession is hard to fight because the central bank can't simply print.

The 19th-century gold standard worked acceptably for stable times but failed catastrophically under WWI strains and the Great Depression. Most countries left it in the 1930s; the international system collapsed completely with Nixon ending US gold convertibility in 1971.

concepts.title: Fiat Money
concepts.contentHtml:
Fiat money has no intrinsic value. A US dollar bill is paper. Its value comes purely from social agreement: people accept it because they expect others to accept it, because the government accepts it for taxes, and because the central bank manages its supply.

This sounds fragile but works remarkably well. Fiat money lets central banks expand or contract supply to match economic conditions — fighting recessions with monetary stimulus, fighting inflation by raising rates.

The cost: the discipline of a finite commodity is gone. If institutions fail or political constraints break down, fiat money can hyperinflate. Weimar Germany, Yugoslavia 1990s, Zimbabwe 2008, Venezuela 2010s. Argentina went through its own hyperinflation in 1989-90.

Most economists view fiat as superior to commodity money under good institutions, but the tradeoff is real: fiat requires trust in the central bank.

concepts.title: Money Aggregates: M0, M1, M2
concepts.contentHtml:
'How much money is in the economy?' depends on what you count.

M0 (or MB, monetary base): physical currency plus commercial bank reserves at the central bank. The narrowest measure.

M1: currency in circulation plus checking deposits and other immediately spendable balances (bank reserves are excluded). Since 2020 the US Fed also counts savings deposits in M1.

M2: M1 plus savings deposits (under the pre-2020 US definition), small time deposits, and retail money market funds. Less liquid but still 'money-ish.'

M3 (no longer published in the US): M2 plus large institutional deposits and other near-money instruments.

The aggregates can move quite differently. After 2008, MB exploded with QE while M2 grew much more slowly — banks held extra reserves rather than lending them out. The gap between base money and broad money is one signal of how the financial system is functioning.

concepts.title: Money as Social Convention
concepts.contentHtml:
The deep philosophical point: money is whatever a society agrees to treat as money. There's no Platonic 'real money'.

Yap stone money — large stone disks, sometimes the size of cars — were the medium of exchange on the Pacific island of Yap. Ownership transferred without physical movement of the stones. One famous stone sat at the bottom of the lagoon and was still treated as money.

Cigarettes circulated as money in WWII POW camps. Mobile phone minutes circulate as money in parts of Africa. Bitcoin functions partly as money for some users.

This means new forms of money can emerge whenever institutions allow. Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), cryptocurrencies, and stablecoins are all attempts to design new monetary forms for new circumstances. Whether they succeed depends on whether they're trusted enough to be widely accepted — exactly the same test that governs traditional money.

title: Banks & Credit Creation
description: Fractional reserve, the money multiplier, balance sheets, endogenous money

concepts.title: What Banks Do
concepts.contentHtml:
A commercial bank takes deposits and makes loans. That sounds simple but has profound consequences.

The bank's balance sheet has assets (loans, securities, reserves at the central bank) and liabilities (deposits, borrowings, equity). The bank's profit comes from the spread: it pays low interest on deposits and earns higher interest on loans.

Banks transform short-term deposits into long-term loans, take on credit risk that depositors avoid, and provide payment services. They're not just intermediaries between savers and borrowers — they actively create the asset side of their balance sheet through lending.

concepts.title: Fractional Reserve Banking
concepts.contentHtml:
Banks don't keep enough cash to pay all depositors at once — they keep only a fraction in reserves (vault cash plus deposits at the central bank), lending the rest out.

The reserve ratio — the fraction of deposits held as reserves — is set by regulation, by the central bank, and increasingly by the bank's own liquidity management. US reserve requirements were lowered to 0% in 2020; banks now manage reserves based on settlement needs, not regulatory minimums.

This is the genius and the danger of banking: a bank turning $100 of deposits into $90 of loans helps fund productive activity, but if all depositors arrived simultaneously to withdraw, there'd be only $10 in cash. Bank runs are baked into the structure.

concepts.title: The Money Multiplier
concepts.contentHtml:
Textbook story: the central bank injects $100 of reserves. A bank lends $90 (keeping $10 reserve). The borrower spends it; the recipient deposits it at another bank. That bank lends $81. And so on.

Total deposits eventually = $100/(reserve ratio). With a 10% ratio, the multiplier is 10. The central bank's $100 created $1,000 of deposits.

Reality is messier. Banks hold excess reserves; some money leaks into cash; loan demand isn't infinite. Post-2008, the US monetary base grew massively while M2 grew much less — the textbook multiplier broke.

The modern view: banks aren't simple multipliers. They lend when they see profitable opportunities, and reserves come along. The causation is more complex than 'reserves cause loans.'

concepts.title: Endogenous Money
concepts.contentHtml:
The endogenous money view, championed by post-Keynesians (and now mostly accepted by central banks): banks create money when they lend, not the other way around.

When a bank issues a $100,000 mortgage, it credits the borrower's deposit account with $100,000. Both the loan (asset) and the deposit (liability) are created out of nothing simultaneously. No reserves were touched.

The bank acquires reserves later — through deposits, interbank borrowing, or central bank operations — to settle inter-bank flows when the borrower spends the money.

The Bank of England's 2014 quarterly bulletin made this explicit: 'Money creation in the modern economy.' The textbook reserve-multiplier story was officially declared misleading.

Implication: monetary policy works mainly through interest rates that affect loan demand, not by directly setting the money supply.

concepts.title: Constraints on Bank Lending
concepts.contentHtml:
If banks create money out of thin air, what stops them from lending infinitely?

Capital requirements: banks must hold equity equal to a fraction of risk-weighted assets. Basel III sets internationally coordinated minimums. Lending more requires more capital.

Profitability: bad loans destroy capital. Banks won't lend to borrowers unlikely to repay.

Liquidity: banks need to fund loans with deposits or other liabilities. If depositors flee, lending capacity shrinks.

Regulation: in many jurisdictions, specific lending types (real estate, leveraged) face direct caps.

Demand: ultimately, someone has to want the loan. In recessions, loan demand collapses regardless of banks' willingness to lend.

Banking system money creation is therefore constrained by capital, prudence, regulation, and the real economy — not by reserves alone. This is why central banks now rely on policy rates rather than monetary aggregate targeting.

title: Central Banks
description: Open market operations, lender of last resort, dual mandates, independence

concepts.title: What Central Banks Do
concepts.contentHtml:
A modern central bank wears several hats simultaneously.

Monetary policy: setting the policy rate to target inflation and (sometimes) output.

Lender of last resort: providing emergency liquidity to banks during crises.

Bank supervision: regulating commercial banks for safety and soundness.

Payment system operator: running the rails on which interbank settlement happens.

Government's bank: holding deposits, issuing debt, managing reserves.

The Federal Reserve, ECB, Bank of Japan, Bank of England, People's Bank of China, and a handful of others run the global financial system. Their decisions ripple into every market.

concepts.title: Open Market Operations
concepts.contentHtml:
The classical lever: open market operations (OMOs). The central bank buys or sells government securities in the secondary market.

Buying bonds → pays for them with newly created reserves → expands the monetary base → tends to lower interest rates.

Selling bonds → drains reserves → contracts the base → tends to raise rates.

Pre-2008, the Fed used small daily OMOs to keep the federal funds rate at its target. The volume needed was tiny relative to the reserve system.

Post-2008, with reserves enormous and at the policy floor, OMOs lost direct relevance for setting short rates — but reemerged in the form of quantitative easing, large-scale asset purchases extending well beyond short-term Treasuries.

concepts.title: Lender of Last Resort
concepts.contentHtml:
Walter Bagehot's 1873 doctrine: in a crisis, the central bank should lend freely, at penalty rates, against good collateral.

Lending freely prevents panic-driven bank runs from destroying solvent institutions. Penalty rates ensure banks don't free-ride on the support — they should prefer market funding when available. Good collateral protects the central bank from credit losses.

This principle was honored in the breach during the 2008 crisis. The Fed lent on weak collateral, at non-penalty rates, to non-bank entities (Bear Stearns, AIG). Critics called it overreach; defenders said the alternative was financial collapse.

Bagehot's principle remains the formal doctrine, but the practice has evolved. The 2008 and 2020 episodes showed central banks willing to do whatever it took, redefining 'last resort' liquidity in real time.

concepts.title: Mandates: Single, Dual, Multiple
concepts.contentHtml:
What is the central bank trying to achieve?

Single mandate (ECB, Bank of England historically, RBNZ original): primarily inflation. The argument: monetary policy can only durably affect inflation, so don't pretend otherwise.

Dual mandate (Federal Reserve since 1977): price stability AND maximum employment. The argument: monetary policy affects output and jobs in the short run, so the central bank should weigh employment too.

Triple/multiple mandates: Australia, Norway include financial stability or exchange rate considerations.

Modern practice has converged in some ways. The Fed's 2020 framework explicitly emphasized employment alongside its 2% inflation target (its 2025 review dialed some of that emphasis back). The Bank of England added 'support government economic policy.' The post-2008 era has put financial stability on every central bank's radar.

The mandate matters in tradeoff moments — when fighting inflation costs employment, the central bank's framing shapes how aggressively it acts.

concepts.title: Independence
concepts.contentHtml:
Most modern central banks are independent: politicians can't directly order them around.

The case: politicians have a chronic incentive to pressure for low rates before elections, generating short-term booms and long-term inflation. Independence shields the central bank from this time inconsistency trap.

Empirically, more-independent central banks have produced lower average inflation without higher unemployment. The 1970s — when central banks were less independent — produced the worst inflation in modern Western history; the 1990s-2010s — when independence peaked — produced 'Great Moderation' stability.

Independence is under pressure now. Trump publicly browbeat Fed chairs. Erdogan repeatedly ousted Turkish central bankers; the lira collapsed. In India, the government clashed with the RBI, whose governor resigned in 2018. Brazil and Argentina have oscillated.

The institutional consensus of 1990-2020 may not survive the next political generation. The best-case argument for it: it's worked. The risk: people forget why we needed it.

title: Monetary Transmission
description: How a policy rate change travels through credit, asset prices, expectations

concepts.title: The Policy Rate as Starting Point
concepts.contentHtml:
The central bank moves one number — the policy rate (federal funds in the US, deposit facility in the eurozone, Bank Rate in the UK).

By itself this rate matters little. What matters is how the change propagates through the rest of the economy: other interest rates, asset prices, exchange rates, credit conditions, and ultimately consumer spending and business investment.

The propagation is called the monetary transmission mechanism. It involves multiple channels operating simultaneously, with long and variable lags.

concepts.title: Interest Rate Channel
concepts.contentHtml:
The most direct channel: the policy rate ripples through the term structure.

Short rates closely track the policy rate. Long rates respond to expected future short rates plus a term premium. So the central bank can move long rates indirectly through expectations management.

Lower rates → cheaper borrowing → more business investment, more home buying, more durable goods purchases (cars, appliances). Higher rates do the reverse.

Investment is generally most sensitive: a few hundred basis points can swing a project from negative to positive NPV. Consumption is less sensitive but still responsive through housing and credit-card debt.

concepts.title: Asset Price Channel
concepts.contentHtml:
Lower discount rates mean higher present values of future cash flows. Stocks, bonds, and real estate all rise.

This creates a wealth effect: households feel richer and spend more. The traditional estimate is roughly 2-5 cents of additional consumption per $1 of wealth gain — small but cumulative across millions of households.

Asset prices also affect investment via Tobin's q: when market values exceed replacement cost, firms have incentive to invest in new capital.

The asset price channel is one reason monetary policy effects are visible quickly in markets but slowly in the real economy. Stocks rebound first; consumption follows; investment lags further.

concepts.title: Exchange Rate Channel
concepts.contentHtml:
Lower domestic rates make the currency less attractive to foreign investors. Capital flows out, currency depreciates.

A weaker currency boosts net exports — foreign goods cost more, domestic goods become more competitive. This raises GDP for the depreciating country.

For small open economies (Sweden, New Zealand, Switzerland) this is the dominant transmission channel. For large economies with relatively closed trade (US, eurozone in aggregate), it's secondary but still significant.

The flip side: currency wars. If everyone tries to devalue simultaneously, no one gains relative competitiveness. Major monetary easings can trigger international friction — quantitative easing in 2010-15 was partly framed as a 'currency war' by emerging markets facing capital inflows.

concepts.title: Long and Variable Lags
concepts.contentHtml:
Milton Friedman's most-quoted phrase: monetary policy operates with 'long and variable lags.'

Empirically, peak effects on output appear 1-2 years after a rate change; effects on inflation peak 2-3 years out. Lags vary across business cycles, financial conditions, and the state of expectations.

This creates an extreme forecasting problem. The central bank must act today based on forecasts of inflation 18 months from now. By the time the economy responds, conditions may have changed. Stop-go monetary policy — over-tightening, then over-easing — has been a recurrent failure.

Lags are the deep reason for rule-based, forward-looking, expectations-managed monetary policy. The central bank can't react to current data; it must anticipate.

This is also why patient stewardship works better than activist micro-management. Trying to fine-tune through lags introduces more noise than signal.

title: Bank Runs & Financial Crises
description: Diamond-Dybvig, contagion, deposit insurance, Lehman and the GFC

concepts.title: The Diamond-Dybvig Model
concepts.contentHtml:
Diamond and Dybvig (1983, Nobel 2022) gave the canonical model of why banks are simultaneously useful and fragile.

Depositors want liquidity (the option to withdraw any time). Borrowers need long-term funding for productive but illiquid investments. Banks bridge the gap by transforming short-term liabilities into long-term assets.

This works as long as depositors don't all show up at once. There are two equilibria: the good one, where each depositor expects others to be patient and rationally stays patient too; and the bad one (a bank run), where each depositor expects others to withdraw and rationally rushes to withdraw first.

Both equilibria are self-fulfilling. A solvent bank can fail simply because depositors believe it might fail. The fragility is structural, not a sign of bad management.

concepts.title: Deposit Insurance
concepts.contentHtml:
The standard fix: deposit insurance. The government guarantees deposits up to some limit ($250,000 in the US since 2008 via FDIC; €100,000 in the EU).

If your deposits are guaranteed, you don't need to run. The bad equilibrium evaporates.

The cost: moral hazard. Insured depositors don't monitor banks for safety. Banks face less market discipline. Combined with leverage, this can encourage excessive risk-taking — the Savings & Loan crisis of the 1980s was partly driven by deposit-insured S&Ls gambling on increasingly bad loans.

The fix to the fix: regulation and supervision. Capital requirements, leverage ratios, on-site examinations, stress tests. Deposit insurance + regulation forms the modern bank-safety architecture, in place across most developed economies since the 1930s-40s.

concepts.title: Contagion
concepts.contentHtml:
Crises spread between banks even when individual banks are sound. Contagion works through several mechanisms.

Direct exposure: if Bank A lends to Bank B, B's failure damages A's balance sheet.

Asset fire sales: a failing bank dumps assets cheaply, depressing prices, making other banks holding similar assets look insolvent.

Information cascades: if Bank B fails, depositors at similar banks suspect their bank too. The bad equilibrium of one bank can pull in others.

Funding markets: when interbank lending dries up, even sound banks lose access to short-term funding.

This is why the 2008 Lehman collapse cascaded so quickly. Contagion turns individual failures into systemic events, justifying interventions (bailouts, emergency lending) far beyond what individual-bank analysis would suggest.

concepts.title: The 2008 Global Financial Crisis
concepts.contentHtml:
The classic case study. Stylized timeline:

2002-06: US housing prices boomed; subprime mortgage lending exploded; risks were repackaged as 'safe' AAA-rated mortgage-backed securities and CDOs.

2007: housing prices peaked and started falling. Subprime defaults rose. Securities tied to them collapsed in value.

2008: losses propagated through the financial system. Bear Stearns failed in March; Lehman in September. A large money market fund 'broke the buck.' AIG required a $182B rescue. The interbank market froze.

Late 2008-09: coordinated TARP bank bailouts, Federal Reserve emergency facilities, fiscal stimulus, eventual stabilization at huge cost in output and unemployment.

The crisis exposed the limits of pre-2008 financial regulation. Shadow banks (money market funds, repo markets, structured investment vehicles) had grown outside the bank-deposit-insurance perimeter. Dodd-Frank (US) and Basel III (international) extended the regulatory net afterward, though debates over financial reform continue.

concepts.title: Lessons and Limits
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-2008 reform agenda emphasized:

Higher capital requirements (Basel III): more equity, less leverage, especially for systemically important banks.

Liquidity rules: banks must hold high-quality liquid assets to survive 30-day stress scenarios.

Resolution authority: tools to wind down failing banks without contagion or bailouts.

Macroprudential supervision: regulators look at systemic risk, not just individual banks.

Stress tests: periodic forward-looking checks on bank resilience to severe scenarios.

These reforms have made the banking system measurably stronger. The 2023 Silicon Valley Bank failure was contained, not catastrophic. But financial crises evolve. New vulnerabilities emerge in fintech, crypto, private credit, central counterparties. Regulators are always partly fighting the last war.

Kindleberger's wisdom: 'There will be another financial crisis. Just don't ask me when.'

title: Currency Regimes
description: Fixed, floating, pegged, dollarized — how countries choose to anchor their money

concepts.title: Floating vs Fixed
concepts.contentHtml:
A country must choose how to handle its currency's value relative to others. Two extremes:

Floating exchange rate: the market sets it daily. Central bank doesn't intervene to defend a particular level.

Fixed exchange rate: the central bank commits to a particular value (often vs the dollar or a basket) and stands ready to buy/sell currency to maintain it.

Most major economies (US, EU, UK, Japan, Australia) float. Most small economies, emerging markets, and resource-dependent economies use various forms of fix or peg.

The choice involves a tradeoff: floating gives independent monetary policy but volatile exchange rates; fixing gives stable exchange rates but ties policy to maintaining the peg.

concepts.title: The Trilemma
concepts.contentHtml:
The Mundell-Fleming trilemma: a country can have at most two of three things at once:

1. Fixed exchange rate

2. Free international capital flows

3. Independent monetary policy

Pick any two; the third must give.

US, eurozone, UK, Japan: independent policy + free capital → floating rate.

Hong Kong: fixed rate (to USD) + free capital → no independent policy (HKMA tracks the Fed).

China (historically): fixed-ish rate + independent policy → capital controls.

The trilemma is binding. Countries that try to violate it eventually face crisis. The 1992 ERM crisis (UK, Italy) and the 1997 Asian crisis came partly from countries trying to fix rates while liberalizing capital flows.

concepts.title: Pegs and Bands
concepts.contentHtml:
Between hard floats and rigid fixes, there's a spectrum.

Hard peg: exchange rate held to a fixed value with strong commitment (currency boards, like Hong Kong).

Soft peg: a target value with some willingness to adjust (Vietnam, parts of the Gulf).

Crawling peg: the target moves predictably over time, often to track inflation differentials.

Band: the currency floats within a corridor; outside the band, the central bank intervenes.

Managed float: nominally floating, but the central bank intervenes to dampen excessive moves.

Reality: most countries' regimes are somewhere in the middle. The IMF maintains a classification, but countries' actual practices often differ from their announced regimes — known as 'fear of floating.'

concepts.title: Dollarization & Currency Boards
concepts.contentHtml:
The most extreme commitments to a foreign anchor.

Dollarization: abandon the domestic currency and adopt a foreign one (usually the US dollar). Ecuador (2000), El Salvador (2001), Zimbabwe (briefly), Panama (longstanding). Loses all monetary autonomy but eliminates exchange-rate risk and currency-driven inflation.

Currency board: issue domestic currency 1:1 backed by foreign reserves at a fixed rate. Hong Kong's most famous, with the HKD pegged to USD since 1983. Argentina ran one 1991-2001 (dollar-peso 1:1) and abandoned it catastrophically.

These regimes credibly anchor inflation by removing the central bank's discretion. The cost: no flexibility. When the anchor currency's monetary policy is wrong for your economy, you have no escape. The Argentine collapse came when domestic conditions diverged so far from the US that the peg became unsustainable.

concepts.title: Choosing a Regime
concepts.contentHtml:
The 'right' regime depends on country characteristics.

Floating works best for large, diversified economies with deep financial markets, credible central banks, and external shocks distinct from trading partners. The benefits of independent monetary policy outweigh exchange-rate volatility costs.

Pegging or dollarizing works best for small, open economies highly integrated with a major trading partner, where credibility is hard to establish (poor monetary track record), and where stable exchange rates are crucial for trade.

Politics also matters. A peg can lock in monetary discipline that domestic politicians can't credibly commit to. Currency boards in the 1990s were partly external commitment devices. Regime choice is endogenous to institutional quality.

The post-Bretton Woods experience: most countries have moved toward more flexible regimes over time, as financial integration deepens and the trilemma binds harder. Pure pegs have become rarer. But complete laissez-faire floating remains exceptional too — most countries 'manage' their currencies in practice even if not in declaration.

title: Reserve Currencies & the Petrodollar
description: Why the world holds dollars — Bretton Woods, the petrodollar bargain, exorbitant privilege, de-dollarization

concepts.title: What a Reserve Currency Is
concepts.contentHtml:
A reserve currency is one held in significant quantities by foreign central banks and used widely in international transactions.

Three roles overlap. Store of value for foreign reserves. Medium of exchange in international trade and finance. Unit of account for commodity prices, debt issuance, and contracts.

Today's distribution: USD ~57% of global reserves, EUR ~20%, JPY/GBP ~5% each, RMB ~2%, others combined ~11%. The USD's dominance has receded modestly over decades but remains overwhelming.

Becoming a reserve currency requires deep financial markets, free capital flows, rule of law, and a credible central bank. Few currencies meet all four conditions; fewer still at scale.

concepts.title: Bretton Woods and the Dollar
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1944 Bretton Woods conference designed the postwar international monetary system. The US dollar was fixed to gold at $35/oz; other major currencies were fixed to the dollar.

The system worked while US gold reserves were ample and US inflation low. By the late 1960s, both conditions failed. US Vietnam War spending and Great Society programs ran the printing press faster than gold reserves grew. Foreign holders increasingly demanded conversion.

August 1971: Nixon unilaterally suspended dollar convertibility. The 'Nixon shock' ended Bretton Woods and ushered in the modern fiat era. By 1973, major currencies were floating against the dollar, and the dollar was pure fiat.

Yet the dollar's reserve role survived — even strengthened. Network effects, market depth, and the absence of credible alternatives kept it dominant.

concepts.title: The Petrodollar System
concepts.contentHtml:
After 1971, a key institutional support for the dollar emerged in oil markets.

In a 1974-75 understanding between the US and Saudi Arabia, OPEC oil exports were priced in dollars. Saudi Arabia recycled its oil revenues into US Treasuries, providing a steady demand for dollar assets. The US in turn provided security guarantees.

The result: every country importing oil needed dollars to pay for it. This generated steady global dollar demand independent of US trade balances or interest rates. The 'petrodollar' was an institutional pillar of dollar reserve status.

The arrangement wasn't a formal treaty but emerged from bilateral diplomacy and persisted through inertia. Oil pricing in dollars became a default convention, reinforced by the depth of dollar markets for oil futures, and by sanctions architecture that made non-dollar oil sales increasingly difficult.

concepts.title: Exorbitant Privilege
concepts.contentHtml:
Valéry Giscard d'Estaing's 1960s phrase — 'exorbitant privilege' — describes the benefits the US gets from issuing the world's reserve currency.

Cheaper borrowing: demand for dollar reserves keeps US interest rates lower than they'd otherwise be, possibly by 50-150 basis points historically.

Seigniorage: the US prints currency that foreigners hold; effectively, an interest-free loan to the US government.

Trade flexibility: the US can run persistent current account deficits because the world wants its currency.

Financial sanctions power: control of dollar clearing gives the US extraordinary leverage over global finance, used in sanctions on Iran, Russia, and others.

The privilege is real but not unlimited. It rests on continuing trust in US institutions and the absence of credible alternatives. Both can erode.

concepts.title: De-Dollarization?
concepts.contentHtml:
'De-dollarization' has been predicted for decades and partially happened — but slowly.

Triggers: the 2022 freezing of Russian central bank reserves accelerated discussion of dollar alternatives. China's RMB internationalization has expanded RMB-denominated trade and lending. The BRICS bloc has discussed alternative payment systems (mBridge, BRICS Pay). Saudi Arabia has discussed pricing some oil sales in yuan.

Counterforces: no alternative reserve currency offers the same depth, liquidity, and rule-of-law features as the dollar. The euro is fragmented; the yuan has capital controls and political risk; gold and Bitcoin lack the institutional infrastructure.

Most analysts see a gradual erosion rather than collapse. Dollar share of reserves has fallen from ~70% in 2000 to ~57% today — a meaningful decline, but no one currency is replacing it. The likely trajectory: a multipolar system where the dollar remains primary but with euros, yuan, and other reserves taking larger shares.

The process is path-dependent and political. A US debt crisis, weaponization of sanctions, or sustained inflation could accelerate it. Stable governance and credible monetary policy could slow it. The next decade may decide more than the last fifty.
